q: The part of the universe which we can see is termed the ____ universe.
e: The visible universe refers to the spherical region of the universe comprising all matter that can be observed from Earth.

q: The actual universe might be bigger than the ____ universe.
e: The entire universe is likely much larger than the visible universe, as light from regions beyond it has not had time to reach us.

q: The part we can see is determined by the ____ of the universe.
e: The observable limit of the universe is defined by the distance light has been able to travel since the universe began.

q: To learn the fundamentals of the universe one needs to study astronomy, astrophysics and cosmology which are three closely related ____.
e: Astronomy, astrophysics, and cosmology are interconnected scientific disciplines focused on understanding the universe.

q: Astrophysics is the branch of astronomy that deals with the physics of the universe, including the physical properties of celestial objects, as well as their interactions and ____.
e: Astrophysics applies the laws of physics to understand the behavior, properties, and interactions of celestial bodies.

q: Among the objects studied are galaxies, stars, planets, exoplanets, the interstellar medium and the cosmic microwave ____.
e: The cosmic microwave background is the residual thermal radiation from the Big Bang, a key subject of astrophysical study.

q: Cosmology studies the universe as a whole and its phenomena at largest ____.
e: Cosmology focuses on the origin, evolution, and eventual fate of the universe on the grandest possible scales.

q: The difference between Astrophysics and Cosmology is the domain and scale of the ____.
e: While astrophysics focuses on individual celestial objects and their physics, cosmology examines the universe as a single, large-scale entity.

q: Astronomy is a natural science that deals with the study of celestial objects, which are any natural bodies outside of the earth's ____.
e: Astronomy encompasses the observation and study of all natural phenomena and objects located beyond Earth's atmosphere.

q: Examples are the Moon, the Sun, planets, stars, comets, nebulae, star clusters and galaxies, ____.
e: These are all examples of celestial objects that fall under the domain of astronomical study.

q: The Earth, our planet is part of the solar system that contains eight planets and the ____.
e: The solar system is gravitationally bound to the Sun, which is the central star orbited by Earth and seven other planets.

q: The Sun is a star and there are many others like it in the ____.
e: The Sun is an average-sized star, and billions of similar stars exist throughout the universe.

q: The closest star to our own is called Proxima Centauri, together with approximately $10^{11}$ other stars they make up the Milky ____.
e: The Milky Way is the barred spiral galaxy that contains our Solar System and an estimated 100 to 400 billion stars.

q: The Milky Way is one of about $10^{11}$ galaxies in the visible ____.
e: Current estimates suggest there are roughly 100 billion galaxies within the observable universe.

q: Therefore, the visible universe consists of roughly $10^{22}$ ____.
e: Multiplying the number of galaxies by the average number of stars per galaxy yields an estimated $10^{22}$ stars in the visible universe.

q: Galaxies cluster into groups; our group is labeled the Local Group and contains about 30 ____.
e: The Local Group is the galaxy group that includes the Milky Way, Andromeda, and approximately 30 other smaller galaxies.

q: The main force holding all of these systems together is ____.
e: Gravity is the dominant fundamental force responsible for binding planets, stars, galaxies, and galaxy clusters together.

q: Astronomers have created units of measurement for astronomical ____.
e: Due to the vast scales involved, astronomers use specialized units like the AU, light year, and parsec to measure distances.

q: One of these units is called an Astronomical Unit (AU), the mean distance between the Earth and the Sun, that is, ____.
e: The Astronomical Unit is a standard unit of length defined as the average distance from the Earth to the Sun.

q: The light year is an another astronomical unit for measuring large ____.
e: A light year is the distance that light travels in a vacuum in one Julian year, used for interstellar and intergalactic distances.

q: The light year (ly) is the distance travelled by light in a vacuum in one ____.
e: By definition, a light year is a measure of distance, not time, equivalent to the distance light covers in one Earth year.

q: One parsec (pc) is the distance to a star that subtends an angle of 1 arc sec (arc second) at an arc length of 1 ____.
e: A parsec is defined using parallax, specifically the distance at which 1 AU subtends an angle of one arcsecond.
One parsec is approximately equal to $3.08 \times 10^{13}$ kilometers.
One parsec is equivalent to approximately 3.26 light years.
One parsec is equal to approximately 206,265 Astronomical Units.

q: Astrophysicists and astronomers have theorized that the universe must have originated at a single point of infinite density and finite time then began to ____.
e: The prevailing cosmological model states that the universe began as a singularity and has been expanding ever since.

q: This is known as the Big Bang ____.
e: The Big Bang theory is the leading scientific explanation for the origin and evolution of the universe.

q: After the initial expansion, the theory maintains that the universe cooled sufficiently to allow the formation of subatomic particles, and later simple ____.
e: As the universe expanded and cooled, quarks formed protons and neutrons, which later captured electrons to form the first simple atoms.

q: Giant clouds of these primordial elements later coalesced through gravity to form stars and ____.
e: Gravitational collapse of primordial gas clouds led to the formation of the first stars, which eventually grouped together to form galaxies.

q: This all began roughly 13.8 billion years ago, and is thus considered to be the ____ of the universe.
e: The time elapsed since the Big Bang, approximately 13.8 billion years, is recognized as the current age of the universe.

q: Age: $1.38 \times 10^{10}$ years (or) 13.799 ____ years.
e: The age of the universe is precisely estimated at 13.799 billion years, which is $1.38 \times 10^{10}$ years.

q: Average temperature: ____ K.
e: The average temperature of the universe, as measured by the cosmic microwave background radiation, is approximately 2.72548 Kelvin.

q: Contents: Ordinary matter (4.9%), Dark matter (23%), Dark energy (____).
e: The universe's mass-energy content is dominated by dark energy (72%), followed by dark matter (23%) and ordinary matter (4.9%).
